en.name: OrgTik identity system
en.summary: A connected identity built to move from strategy into every useful touchpoint.
en.transformation: From a strong mark to a complete, flexible brand experience.
en.challenge: OrgTik began with a distinctive mark but no system around it. Each new page, deck and product screen was designed from scratch, so the brand looked slightly different every time it appeared.
en.goal: Build one identity that could carry a studio and a software company at once: recognizable as a favicon, confident on signage, and simple enough for anyone on the team to use.
en.role: Brand strategy, identity design, visual system, guidelines, and the first wave of digital and print applications.

title: From sketch
to system.
approach.intro: Five stages took the identity from a single mark to a system the whole team can use without us in the room.

steps.title: Listen
steps.detail: We collected every existing touchpoint, spoke with the founders, and mapped where the brand held together and where it drifted.

steps.title: Distill
steps.detail: The positioning became three design principles: clear, connected and calm. Every later decision was tested against them.

steps.title: Shape
steps.detail: We refined the mark for small sizes, paired it with a horizontal lockup, and built a plum-and-violet palette with Montserrat as the single type family.

steps.title: Apply
steps.detail: Instead of polishing in isolation, we tested the system on cards, screens, signage and social templates while it was still flexible.

steps.title: Guide
steps.detail: The system shipped as guidelines, a shared asset library, and editable templates so it stays consistent as the business grows.

title: One identity,
every touchpoint.
delivered.intro: The core of the system: a mark, a palette with tested contrast pairs, one type family, and the applications it was proven on.

title: What changed
for the team.
results.intro: Design outcomes are measured in consistency and speed: how quickly a new asset can be made, and how reliably it looks like OrgTik.

metrics.label: faster to produce a new branded asset

shifts: Each asset designed from a blank page
Templates that start most of the way there
The logo used in five different ways
Two lockups with clear usage rules
One palette with tested contrast pairs

en.name: Connected platform concept
en.summary: A product direction for bringing six everyday systems into one coherent workspace.
en.transformation: From disconnected tools to one clearer operating picture.
en.challenge: Teams juggled separate tools for people, clients, files, tasks, marketing and the website. Each had its own login, its own data, and its own idea of who a customer was.
en.goal: Design and prototype one workspace where six systems share records, permissions and navigation, without forcing teams to change how they already work.
en.role: Product discovery, technical architecture, interface system and a working frontend prototype.

title: Built in sprints,
shipped in steps.
approach.intro: Five two-to-three-week sprints, each ending with something working that the team could click through and challenge.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.detail: Mapped six tools, 23 recurring workflows, and every place data was copied between them by hand.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.detail: Defined a shared data model for people, clients, files and tasks, plus one contract every module plugs into.

steps.title: Workspace shell
steps.detail: Built single sign-in, global navigation, search and notifications so every module feels like part of one product.

steps.title: Module integration
steps.detail: Connected the six modules to shared records, so a client created in Relationships appears in Work and Files straight away.

steps.title: Hardening
steps.detail: Added automated tests, an accessibility review, performance budgets and a staged release plan.

title: One core,
six connected modules.
delivered.intro: Every module reads from and writes to the same shared layer, so records, access and search stay consistent across the workspace.

title: Measured before
it shipped.
results.intro: Engineering results come from audits and test runs on the prototype, not from opinions about how it feels.

metrics.label: largest contentful paint on a mid-range phone
automated test coverage on shared services

en.title: Connected platform concept
en.description: A product direction for bringing six everyday systems into one coherent workspace.

en.name: Managed digital presence
en.summary: A connected service model spanning the website, hosting, monitoring, and ongoing improvement.
en.transformation: From launch-day delivery to a dependable long-term digital partnership.
en.challenge: The website sat on low-cost shared hosting with manual updates and no tested backups. Pages were slow, plugins were months out of date, and nobody was watching when something went wrong.
en.goal: Move the website to a managed home with monitoring, verified backups and a named person to call, using a planned, low-risk switch.
en.role: Hosting audit, migration plan, environment setup, DNS cutover, monitoring, backups and ongoing performance care.

title: A runbook,
not a leap of faith.
approach.intro: Every migration step was written down, checked and reversible before anything live was touched.

steps.title: Audit
steps.detail: Listed the site, plugins, DNS records, email routing and every third-party script it depended on.

steps.title: Staging
steps.detail: Built a staging copy on the new environment and tested every page and form against the original.

steps.title: Safety net
steps.detail: Took full backups and wrote a rollback plan before any live change was made.

steps.title: Migrate
steps.detail: Moved files and database in a planned low-traffic window, then compared both versions page by page.

steps.title: Cutover
steps.detail: Switched DNS with short cache times, renewed SSL and confirmed that email kept flowing.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Turned on monitoring, daily backups and update routines, with alerts routed to a named person.

title: Everything watched,
nothing assumed.
delivered.intro: The managed setup the site now runs on, shown the way our status view reports it.

title: Faster, and
looked after.
results.intro: Hosting results are tracked week by week: speed after the move, and the care routines that keep it there.

en.title: Managed digital presence
en.description: A connected service model spanning the website, hosting, monitoring, and ongoing improvement.

en.name: Campaign growth system
en.summary: A mock campaign system connecting audience decisions, content, publishing, and the learning loop.
en.transformation: From scattered activity to a campaign rhythm the whole team can see.
en.team: Strategy, content, paid media and analytics
en.challenge: The firm was posting, advertising and emailing, but each channel ran on its own. Nobody could say which activity produced a qualified enquiry, so budget followed habit rather than results.
en.goal: Connect audience, content, publishing and reporting into one campaign rhythm, and prove which channels create qualified leads.
en.role: Audit and baseline, audience strategy, campaign creative, paid and organic management, and monthly performance reporting.

title: Twelve weeks,
one campaign rhythm.
approach.intro: Phases overlapped on purpose: tracking came first, and budget only moved once the data could show what was working.

steps.title: Audit & baseline
steps.detail: Connected analytics, cleaned up tracking and recorded a three-month baseline for every channel.

steps.title: Audience & message
steps.detail: Interviewed the sales team, defined two priority audiences and wrote one message for each stage of the decision.

steps.title: Content system
steps.detail: Built reusable templates and a weekly publishing calendar so every channel told the same story.

steps.title: Launch
steps.detail: Launched paid search and LinkedIn with small test budgets and agreed success criteria.

steps.title: Optimize & learn
steps.detail: Moved budget each week toward the ads and topics that produced qualified leads, not just clicks.

title: A weekly rhythm
the team can see.
delivered.intro: The campaign system that replaced one-off posts: every day has a job, and every channel feeds the same report.

title: The numbers
behind the rhythm.
results.intro: Baseline months are compared with campaign months on the same tracking, so every change is measured like for like.

en.title: Campaign growth system
en.description: A mock campaign system connecting audience decisions, content, publishing, and the learning loop.

en.name: Support continuity system
en.summary: A mock support experience that makes requests, priorities, fixes, and follow-up easier to understand.
en.transformation: From reactive fixes to a visible rhythm of care and improvement.
en.challenge: Requests arrived by email, phone and hallway conversation. Urgent problems waited behind small ones, the same issues came back every few weeks, and nobody could see what had already been tried.
en.goal: Give the team one place to ask for help, priorities everyone agrees on, and fixes that stay fixed.
en.role: Support audit, intake and triage design, root-cause fixes, knowledge base, and a monthly care rhythm.

title: Every step,
logged like a ticket.
approach.intro: We treated the support set-up itself as a series of tickets: each one opened with a problem and closed with a change.

steps.title: Audit the requests
steps.detail: Reviewed three months of requests and grouped 214 tickets by cause. Four root causes created more than half of the volume.

steps.title: One way to ask
steps.detail: Replaced scattered emails with one request form that captures device, urgency and screenshots up front.

steps.title: Agree priorities
steps.detail: Set four priority levels with response targets, so urgent problems move first and everyone knows what to expect.

steps.title: Fix and document
steps.detail: Fixed the four root causes and wrote a short knowledge-base article for each, so the next person solves it in minutes.

steps.title: Review and improve
steps.detail: A monthly care report shows volume, response times and what we improved, before small issues become big ones.

title: Clear priorities,
clear promises.
delivered.intro: The priority model agreed with the team. Every request is sorted on arrival, and every level has a response target.

title: Before and after,
side by side.
results.intro: Support results compare the three months before the change with the three months after, using the same request log.

en.title: Support continuity system
en.description: A mock support experience that makes requests, priorities, fixes, and follow-up easier to understand.

en.name: When a website becomes part of the operating system
en.excerpt: A practical way to connect customer experience, team workflow, and the tools behind both.
takeaways: Treat the website as part of how the business runs, not a separate brochure.
Map the hand-offs between customer actions and team workflows before choosing tools.
Start with one connected journey and extend from there.

sections.heading: The website is already an operating tool
paragraphs: Every enquiry form, booking request and product page starts work somewhere inside the business. When the website is treated as a standalone brochure, that work arrives without context and someone has to re-type, forward or chase it.
Seeing the website as part of the operating system changes the brief: the question is no longer only how a page looks, but what happens after someone uses it.

sections.heading: Map the hand-offs first
paragraphs: Before choosing tools, list the moments where a customer action becomes internal work: a request becomes a lead, a lead becomes a project, a project creates documents and follow-ups.
For each hand-off, note who picks it up, what information they need and where it currently gets lost. That map is more valuable than any feature list.

sections.heading: Connect one journey at a time
paragraphs: Trying to connect everything at once usually stalls. Pick the journey that costs the most time today — often enquiry to first reply — and connect it end to end.
Once that journey works, the next one is easier, because the shared records and habits already exist.

en.title: When a website becomes part of the operating system
en.description: A practical way to connect customer experience, team workflow, and the tools behind both.

en.name: A brand system should make the next decision easier
en.excerpt: How a useful identity creates consistency without making every touchpoint feel the same.
takeaways: A brand system is a set of decisions, not a collection of files.
Define the few rules that matter most and make them easy to apply.
Give room for variation so touchpoints do not all look the same.

sections.heading: Consistency is a side effect, not the goal
paragraphs: Teams often ask for consistency when what they really want is fewer debates. A useful brand system answers the recurring questions — which colour, which type size, which tone — before they are asked.
When those answers are clear, consistency follows without every piece looking identical.

sections.heading: Decide the few rules that matter
paragraphs: Most brands need a small core: how the logo behaves, the palette and its ratios, one or two typefaces with clear roles, and a voice that can be described in a sentence.
Everything else can be guidance rather than law. Fewer hard rules make the system easier to adopt.

sections.heading: Design for the next decision
paragraphs: A good test for any guideline is whether it makes the next decision easier for someone who was not in the room. If it needs a meeting to interpret, it is not finished yet.
Review the system after real use: which rules were followed naturally, and which were quietly ignored? The ignored ones usually need to be simpler.

en.title: A brand system should make the next decision easier
en.description: How a useful identity creates consistency without making every touchpoint feel the same.

en.name: Five questions to ask before choosing managed hosting
en.excerpt: Look beyond storage and compare the care, recovery, monitoring, and support around the service.
takeaways: Compare the care around hosting, not only the server specification.
Ask how recovery works before you ever need it.
Make sure support knows the website, not just the infrastructure.

sections.heading: 1. What happens when something breaks?
paragraphs: Ask who notices first, how you are told and what the typical steps to recovery look like. A clear, honest answer is worth more than a headline availability figure.

sections.heading: 2. How are backups taken and tested?
paragraphs: Backups only matter if they can be restored. Ask how often they run, where they are stored, and when a restore was last tested end to end.

sections.heading: 3. Who looks after updates?
paragraphs: Platforms, plugins and dependencies need regular care. Clarify what is updated automatically, what is reviewed first and who checks the website afterwards.

sections.heading: 4. How is performance watched?
paragraphs: Monitoring should cover what visitors experience, not only whether the server is up. Ask which signals are tracked and what happens when they drift.

sections.heading: 5. Does support understand your website?
paragraphs: The most useful support comes from people who know how the website was built and why. Hosting that sits close to the team that designed and maintains the site shortens every conversation.

en.title: Five questions to ask before choosing managed hosting
en.description: Look beyond storage and compare the care, recovery, monitoring, and support around the service.

en.name: Campaigns work better when the system is visible
en.excerpt: Connect the brief, audience, content, decisions, and learning loop before activity accelerates.
takeaways: Write the brief before production starts, not after.
Keep audience, message, channel and owner visible in one place.
Close every campaign with a learning that informs the next one.

sections.heading: Activity is not a strategy
paragraphs: Busy campaign calendars can hide a lack of direction. When each post, ad and email is planned in isolation, it becomes hard to say what worked and why.
A visible system connects every piece of activity to the decision it is meant to support.

sections.heading: One brief, shared early
paragraphs: A short brief — the goal, the audience, the core message, the channels and the owner — gives everyone the same starting point. It also makes it easier to say no to work that does not fit.
Keep the brief where the team already works, so it is referenced rather than forgotten.

sections.heading: Build the learning loop in
paragraphs: Decide up front which signal will tell you whether the campaign is working, and when you will look at it. Then record what you learned, even when the answer is inconclusive.
Over time, those small notes become the most valuable marketing asset a team has.

en.title: Campaigns work better when the system is visible
en.description: Connect the brief, audience, content, decisions, and learning loop before activity accelerates.

en.name: Designing a website that can change without losing itself
en.excerpt: A clear hierarchy and reusable patterns help a website evolve without accumulating visual debt.
takeaways: Plan for the website to change from the first day.
A clear hierarchy and reusable patterns prevent visual debt.
Give content owners guardrails instead of blank canvases.

sections.heading: Every website changes
paragraphs: New services, new team members and new priorities all end up on the website. Designs that only work for launch-day content start to fray within months.
Designing for change means assuming the content will grow, shrink and move — and making that easy.

sections.heading: Patterns over pages
paragraphs: Instead of designing every page from scratch, define a small set of sections that can be combined: an introduction, a feature list, a story, a call to action. Each should work with more or less content than planned.
New pages then become new combinations, not new designs, and the visual language stays coherent.

sections.heading: Guardrails for the people who edit
paragraphs: Content owners need freedom within limits. Sensible defaults, clear field labels and a preview that matches the live site prevent most layout problems before they happen.
The best measure of success is simple: the site still looks considered a year after launch.

en.title: Designing a website that can change without losing itself
en.description: A clear hierarchy and reusable patterns help a website evolve without accumulating visual debt.

en.name: Performance budgets belong in the design conversation
en.excerpt: Media, motion, type, and interaction decisions shape perceived speed long before deployment.
takeaways: Performance is shaped by design decisions long before development.
Agree a budget for media, motion and fonts early.
Measure what visitors feel, not only what tools score.

sections.heading: Speed is a design outcome
paragraphs: Large hero media, many font weights and heavy animation all have a cost. By the time a design reaches development, most of the performance picture has already been decided.
Bringing performance into the design conversation early avoids painful trade-offs later.

sections.heading: Set a budget together
paragraphs: A simple budget — how much media per page, how many font files, which interactions may animate — gives designers and developers a shared constraint to work within.
The budget is not a limit on ambition; it is a way to spend weight where it matters most.

sections.heading: Measure perceived speed
paragraphs: Visitors judge speed by how quickly they can read and act, not by a single score. Watch how soon the main content appears, whether the layout jumps and how responsive the first interactions feel.
Review these signals after every significant change, so the website stays fast as it evolves.

en.title: Performance budgets belong in the design conversation
en.description: Media, motion, type, and interaction decisions shape perceived speed long before deployment.
